title: Insight | Gloco.ai’s Zhang Ning: AI Strengthens Cross-Border Compliance for Go-Global Firms
summary: AI and go-global define this year’s twin headlines; using AI to open overseas markets is widely seen as Chinese firms’ largest near-term opportunity. As merchants scale abroad, cross-border compliance has become acute — and Silicon Valley startup Gloco.ai has stepped into that
author: Unique Research
html:
Unique Research · Insight / Unique Go-Global special · December 12, 2023 · Author (CN): Hong An · Guest: Zhang Ning, Founder & CEO, Gloco.ai

AI and go-global define this year’s twin headlines; using AI to open overseas markets is widely seen as Chinese firms’ largest near-term opportunity. As merchants scale abroad, cross-border compliance has become acute — and Silicon Valley startup Gloco.ai has stepped into that gap.

Commercial since February 2022, Gloco.ai sells AI-driven compliance to SMBs operating globally: legal, accounting, tax, HR, and other admin support. The founding team mixes seasoned cross-border lawyers with top ML/AI talent across four offices spanning time zones and major languages, backed by thousands of local professionals in 20+ countries. In 2023 alone Gloco.ai completed 10,000+ enterprise orders across 200+ service types in 28 countries. Unique Research spoke with founder & CEO Zhang Ning.

AI-powered compliance at better price/performance

Overseas merchants face destination laws and platform policies. Pain points: hard to find local law/accounting/HR firms; fees too high when found; quality uncontrollable once engaged — all can destroy overseas ops. Gloco.ai’s one-stop platform covers entity formation and HR, accounting/tax, IP registration, and a compliance database.

Credentialed lawyers and accountants — including alumni of major firms — use Gloco.ai co-pilot tools plus process automation to keep quality stable under volume. LLM-built compliance profiles auto-collect and pre-process filings, unify expert handoffs (no re-submitting materials), and AI-triage basic Q&A — cutting both sides’ time cost so once-expensive compliance becomes affordable. Big-data + public government data clarify process and pricing across legal/accounting/tax/HR/licensing; for recurring work (tax filings, annual reviews) the platform flags policy changes and proactively proposes responses.

Quality control uses multi-expert review on the same task to find best practice, then trains AI to take repetitive slices — something classical high-cost compliance could not afford. Without such a platform, merchants who discover a weak vendor mid-engagement often have no practical exit.

Product roadmap: deeper LLM use for latent customer need and cross-language communication, plus letting lawyers/accountants offload junior-associate work; LLMs can also reduce subjective inconsistency across practitioners and encode best practice.

Go-global is mainstream; LatAm shows outsized potential

From Gloco.ai’s book, going abroad is increasingly inevitable: domestic demand growth is slower, while Chinese industries sit at world frontiers — not only manufacturing capacity, but software, games, and services exporting this year. Latin America growth has been stronger than expected: large populations drive consumer demand; like Southeast Asia, many merchants care about manufacturing cost and logistics (Mexico’s proximity to the U.S. plus local industrial base). Roughly ~50% of merchants on leading LatAm e-commerce platforms are Chinese. LatAm is a Gloco.ai focus region; demand clusters around company formation and tax (local tax IDs, strict regimes).

Core compliance pain points

In practice Chinese firms often act only after platform or government penalties — weak foresight that creates a market of cheap, low-quality vendors (undertrained staff, even falsified materials) who meet only the minimum bar and ignore long-term ops. Merchants also struggle to price compliance risk. Zhang’s view: compliance is rigid demand — if you spend marketing dollars overseas, you cannot afford platform or local penalties. Platforms currently push risk onto sellers; their power leaves small sellers with little recourse. Many IP complaints chase profit or rival-suppression more than genuine IP protection.

Cost of non-compliance

A large recent shock: USPTO found mass Chinese trademark non-compliance (agents skipping lawyers), canceling tens of thousands of marks and risking store closures and frozen funds. Overseas litigation — especially U.S. IP — is common; Chinese companies are sued repeatedly. During suits products may be unsellable on Amazon; platforms may hold funds and force settlements. Future government focus: tax first (every state needs revenue), then data security/privacy, while bank-account opening grows harder — policies that attract foreign capital yet keep tax and funds onshore.

Tech change vs local professionals

LLMs lower language and knowledge barriers and improve need-understanding across regimes — but compliance is bound to national self-protection; local lawyers, accountants, and tax pros remain essential. Tech remakes the industry through human–AI collaboration rather than full replacement.

Stricter oversight — prepare early

Over 20 years Zhang watched participants shift from large companies to SMBs. Before Amazon, Shopify, cross-border SaaS, Facebook/TikTok, and global-employment platforms, trade needed bilingual talent and large clients. Demand for cross-border legal work now grows every year faster than firms or solo lawyers can serve — and SMBs cannot pay classic hourly rates. Governments trend more protectionist: once-allowed sectors get banned; trust in foreign products/companies fell over the past decade across finance and IP. Tech and product flows remain inevitable — restricted China→U.S. sourcing historically rerouted via Mexico shelling — so firms that master compliant market entry earn premium margins while cost-intolerant rivals exit.

— END —
